content: SHC-transforming protein 1, encoded by the SHC1 gene in humans, plays a critical role in regulating apoptosis and drug resistance in mammalian cells. Structurally, SHC1 belongs to the SH2 domain family, as classified by SCOP. The SHC1 gene is located on chromosome 1 and produces three main protein isoforms: p66SHC, p52SHC, and p46SHC. These isoforms differ in their molecular weights, activities, and subcellular localizations. The p66SHC isoform is the longest and contains an additional N-terminal CH2 domain, while p52SHC and p46SHC are involved in linking activated receptor tyrosine kinases to the RAS signaling pathway. All three isoforms share a common domain structure, including an N-terminal phosphotyrosine-binding (PTB) domain and a C-terminal Src-homology 2 (SH2) domain. These domains enable binding to tyrosine-phosphorylated proteins, although their phosphopeptide-binding specificities differ. Overexpression of SHC proteins has been associated with cancer-related processes, including mitogenesis, carcinogenesis, and metastasis. SHC proteins and their adaptor functions mediate signaling from cell surface receptors such as EGFR, erbB-2, and insulin receptors. Specifically, p52SHC and p46SHC activate the Ras-ERK pathway, while p66SHC inhibits ERK1/2 activity and counteracts the mitogenic and survival properties of T-lymphoma Jurkat cells. Increased levels of p66SHC promote stress-induced apoptosis and regulate oxidative stress-mediated apoptosis through redox signaling pathways. Both p52SHC and p66SHC have been implicated in steroid hormone-regulated cancers and metastasis. SHC1 is also involved in signaling downstream of epidermal growth factor (EGF) stimulation. Upon EGF activation, SHC1 binds to tyrosine kinase receptors on the cell surface via its phosphotyrosine-binding domains. This interaction activates survival pathways and initiates a sub-network of proteins involved in cytoskeletal reorganization, intracellular trafficking, and signal termination. The protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN122 acts as a molecular switch, redirecting SHC1 to SgK269-mediated pathways that regulate cell invasion and morphogenesis. SHC1 is not a static scaffold protein; its conformation dynamically changes over time, modulating the output of EGFR signaling. The regulation of SHC proteins is influenced by the Multiple Copies in T-cell malignancy (MCT-1) protein. MCT-1 modulates the SHC-Ras-ERK pathway, and its reduction leads to decreased phosphorylation of Ras, MEK, and ERK1/2, as well as reduced cyclin D1 levels. MCT-1 depletion also significantly reduces the expression of all three SHC isoforms, with p66SHC being the most affected. This suggests that MCT-1 acts as an inducer of SHC gene transcription. Downregulation of SHC expression following MCT-1 depletion has been observed in tumorigenic processes. Blocking MCT-1 activity could potentially inhibit the SHC signaling cascade and reduce the oncogenic and tumorigenic effects mediated by SHC expression. Oxidative stress, characterized by an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and their elimination, is regulated in part by SHC1. SHC proteins, through tyrosine phosphorylation, participate in growth factorand stress-induced ERK activation. Studies have suggested a link between oxidative stress resistance, extended lifespan, and p66SHC. In mice, p66SHC has been associated with oxidative stress responses and longevity, potentially through its interaction with the DAF-2 insulin-like receptor in the IIS pathway. The p66SHC isoform functions as a redox enzyme involved in apoptotic cell death and is linked to the sirtuin-1 system, endothelial damage, and vascular repair. It plays a role in vascular homeostasis and oxidative stress regulation. Alterations in glucose metabolism and vascular senescence can modulate p66SHC activity. For instance, hyperglycemia-induced protein kinase C activation leads to p66SHC induction, resulting in oxidative stress. Conversely, inhibition of p66SHC by protease-activated protein C exerts a protective effect on diabetic nephropathy. Deletion of p66SHC reduces cardiomyocyte death, preserves cardiac stem cells from oxidative damage, and prevents diabetic cardiomyopathy. Additionally, p66SHC deletion protects against ischemia/reperfusion brain injuries by reducing free radical production. Clinically, SHC signaling activation is implicated in tumorigenesis and cancer progression. SHC proteins, particularly p66SHC, may serve as prognostic markers and therapeutic targets in cancer treatment. SHC1 interacts with SgK269, a member of the Src kinase signaling network, which is associated with basal breast cancer cells. Overexpression of SgK269 in mammary epithelial cells promotes cell growth and may contribute to the progression of aggressive breast cancers. In prostate and ovarian cancers, increased p66SHC expression enhances cell proliferation and tumorigenicity, particularly in prostate cancer xenografts. This tumorigenic effect is linked to p66SHC's ability to increase redox stress in cancer cells.
